summary.title: Embedded Rules of Thumb
summary.one_liner: A curated list of heuristics for embedded systems and software engineering covering design, cost, scheduling, hardware, reuse, optimization, interrupts, and function point estimates, each attributed to sources like Jack Ganssle, Akin's Laws, and Barry Boehm.
keywords: software cost per line of code
takeaways: Keep interrupt service routines small, defer complex work to non-ISR code, and avoid locks, allocation, and blocking calls inside handlers.
Optimize only after profiling; algorithmic changes usually beat micro-optimizations, and clarity should not be sacrificed without measured gains.
Loading a processor above about 70-90% sharply increases development time, so adding hardware can reduce software effort.
Reuse code only after it has been used several times; apply the rule of three before extracting duplicated code into a procedure.
Treat cost and schedule claims (such as $15-$40 per line of code and function point formulas) as rough approximations from cited sources.
summary.summary: The page is a collection of rules of thumb, heuristics, and guidelines for embedded and software development, organized into sections such as General, Design, Cost, Scheduling, Hardware, Software Reuse, Optimization, Red Flags, Interrupts, and Function Point estimates. Each item is a short bullet, many attributed to people such as Jack Ganssle, Akin's Laws, Steve McConnell, and Barry Boehm, with some quoted at length. The author notes the rules are approximations meant to guide thinking rather than strict truths. It ends with a Further Reading list of related rule-of-thumb resources and a revision history.
